**Meigs Syndrome:** Meigs syndrome is a condition characterised by a triad of:

items.text: Ovarian fibroma (fibrothecoma)
Ascites

blocks.text: Liquid-based cytology is often used to collect specimens, including urine, and study cells for various diagnostic purposes.

**Liquid-based cytology:** It is a technique to collect and prepare cell samples for microscopic analysis. It involves gathering cells from various body fluids, such as cervical or vaginal fluids, respiratory secretions, or urine, depending on the diagnostic goal. This method is commonly used for cervical cancer screening.

Cells collected from the cervix with a brush or spatula are suspended in a preservative solution. This suspension is used to prepare slides for cytological examination to detect abnormalities or disease.
**Advantages of Liquid-Based Cytology (LBC):**

items.text: **Improved slide preparation:** LBC creates a thin-layer or monolayer slide preparation, providing better quality and clarity than conventional Papanicolaou (Pap) smears.
**Enhanced cell preservation:** The collection fluid used in LBC fixes, homogenizes, and rinses the cells, ensuring better preservation for microscopic examination.
**Reduced sample contamination:** The homogenization process minimizes the presence of non-representative material, such as blood or mucus, leading to a more accurate analysis of the collected cells.
**Increased diagnostic accuracy:** With improved sample quality, LBC enhances the sensitivity and specificity of cervical cancer screening, allowing for more reliable detection of abnormalities.

blocks.text: **Disadvantage:** Although cervical cytological screening has proven effective in reducing the incidence and mortality of cervical cancer, the conventional Pap test is less sensitive than commonly thought. The false-negative rate of the conventional Pap test has been reported to reach as high as 50%.

Eosin B is not a constituent of the Papanicolaou stain. Eosin is a different type of stain typically used for general histology to highlight cytoplasm in tissues, but it is not used in the Papanicolaou (Pap) stain. The Papanicolaou (Pap) stain is a widely used technique for examining cells from the cervix to screen for cervical cancer and other abnormalities.
It uses a combination of multiple dyes to differentiate cellular components:

items.text: Hematoxylin - Stains the cell nuclei, allowing for clear visualization of nuclear structure.
Orange G - Stains keratinized cells orange, highlighting squamous cells.
Eosin A - Second counterstain & a polychrome mixture of Eosin Y and Light Green (stains cytoplasm and helps differentiate between various cell types).

blocks.text: The presence of ascites, omental caking, a solid adnexal mass, elevated CA-125, and chronic vague symptoms strongly points to serous ovarian tumor.
**Types of Epithelial Ovarian Tumor:**

rows: Serous Cystadenoma: Benign, unilateral, cystic spaces with serous epithelium.
Serous Cystadenocarcinoma: Malignant, often bilateral, cystic and solid components.
Mucinous Cystadenoma: Benign, unilateral, filled with mucinous fluid.
Mucinous Cystadenocarcinoma: Malignant, unilateral, mucinous epithelial lining.
May rupture and spread to the peritoneum.
Endometrioid Carcinoma: Arises from endometrial-like tissue, solid and cystic.
Solid and cystic components, associated with endometriosis.
Clear Cell Carcinoma: Clear cytoplasm due to glycogen accumulation.
Brenner Tumor: Transitional epithelial cells resembling urinary tract epithelium.

items.text: **Mucinous ovarian tumor (Option B):** typically presents as a large, unilateral, multiloculated cystic mass and is less commonly associated with peritoneal spread or omental caking. CA-125 elevation is not as prominent unless the disease is advanced, and it lacks the classic imaging and spread pattern seen in serous carcinoma.

**Granulosa cell tumors (Option D):** are sex cord-stromal tumors that secrete estrogen and often cause hormonal symptoms like abnormal uterine bleeding; they rarely cause ascites or omental caking, and CA-125 is typically not elevated.

blocks.text: The ovarian tumor showing Call-Exner bodies on histopathology is most consistent with a Granulosa Cell Tumor, a type of Sex Cord-Stromal Tumors, for which inhibin serves as an important diagnostic marker.

blocks.text: The given histopathological image shows features suggestive of testicular seminoma.

**Histology of seminoma:** Sheets of monomorphic cells. The sheets are divided into poorly demarcated lobules by the septa of the fibrous tissue. The septa show lymphocytic infiltration (T lymphocytes). The classic seminoma cell is large and round to polyhedral with a distinct cell membrane and a large, central nucleus with one or two prominent nucleoli.
The cytoplasm is clear or watery appearing and contains glycogen. The arrows in the image below show seminomatous tumour cells.
**Seminoma:** It is the most common germ cell tumour of the testis. A similar presentation in the ovary is called dysgerminoma, and germinoma is present in the pineal gland.

items.text: **Incidence:** Peak incidence in the fourth decade.
**Genetics:** Seminomas contain isochromosome 12p and express OCT3/4 & NANOG.

**Gross:** Seminoma has a homogeneous, grey-white, lobulated cut surface, usually devoid of haemorrhage or necrosis. Generally, the tunica albuginea is not penetrated, but extension to the epididymis, spermatic cord, or scrotal sac occasionally occurs.

blocks.text: Serous cystadenocarcinoma is the most common malignant epithelial ovarian tumour, often bilateral, and tends to be multiloculated with papillary projections. CA-125 is a tumour marker for epithelial ovarian cancers, especially serous and endometrioid types. A very high CA-125 (>1000 U/mL) is far more suggestive of malignancy than benign lesions. Patients often present with abdominal distension, ascites, and an adnexal mass.
**Incorrect Options:**

items.text: **Serous cystadenoma (Benign epithelial tumour) (Option A):** Usually unilocular or mildly multilocular, with thin walls and clear serous fluid. CA-125 levels may be normal or only mildly elevated, not usually >1000. There is no invasive growth, and it occurs in younger women compared to cystadenocarcinoma.

**Mature teratoma (Dermoid cyst) (Option B):** Benign germ cell tumour containing ectodermal derivatives like hair, teeth, and sebaceous material. It usually occurs in younger women (teens to early adulthood). CA-125 is not a typical marker; instead, you might find elevated AFP or β-hCG in other germ cell tumours (not teratomas). On imaging, it often has fat-fluid levels or calcifications, not a multiloculated cystic appearance.

**Granulosa cell tumour (Sex cord–stromal tumour) (Option C):** Often estrogen-producing may cause precocious puberty in children or postmenopausal bleeding in older women. Serum marker: Inhibin (not CA-125). Usually, a solid or cystic-solid mass, not a multiloculated cyst with such high CA-125.

blocks.text: **Extra-gonadal germ cell tumor:** The most common site for an extragonadal germ cell tumor is the mediastinum. Extragonadal germ cell tumors can be benign or malignant.
**Benign extragonadal germ cell tumors are called benign teratomas:** These are more common than malignant extragonadal germ cell tumors and are often very large.
Malignant extragonadal germ cell tumors are divided into two types:

items.text: Seminoma
Non-seminoma

blocks.text: Lactiferous ducts are not a part of the TDLU. The morpho-functional unit of the breast is the terminal duct lobular unit(TDLU). TDLU is a grapelike cluster of small alveoli that comprises lobule and terminal duct. A lobule is a collection of multiple ductules, which are epithelial structures that produce milk during lactation.
Terminal ducts consist of 2 parts:

items.text: **Intralobular terminal duct:** A portion of the terminal duct located within the lobule.
**Extralobular terminal duct:** is the portion connecting the lobule to the lactiferous duct.

blocks.text: The patient presenting with breast pain, nipple discharge, and palpable subareolar mass most likely has duct ectasia. Mammary duct ectasia is a benign, non-proliferative breast disease that affects large ducts. It is most common in women who are nearing menopause, typically between the ages of 45 and 55. The breast ducts become clogged with thick secretion and debris, leading to dilation of the duct.
**Symptoms:**

items.text: Nipple discharge, which can be clear, green, brown, or bloody
Breast tenderness or pain, especially around the nipple
A tender lump in the subareolar or periareolar region of a breast
Inward retraction of the nipple due to repeated episodes and scarring

blocks.text: A transverse slit-like or fish-mouth-like retraction of the nipple is classically seen in periductal mastitis but circumferential retraction may indicate a carcinoma.
Ductal ectasia is often diagnosed during a routine mammogram or breast exam and managed by excision. If a lump is found, a biopsy may be needed to rule out cancer.

Alcohol is a major risk factor in Zuska’s disease along with smoking. Zuska’s disease is also known as Squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts(SMOLD), recurrent subareolar abscess, or periductal mastitis. The risk factors include a deficiency of vitamin A associated with smoking(90% of cases).
This leads to k eratinizing squamous metaplasia of the ductal epithelium, which is cuboidal. Keratin released from these cells blocks the ductal system.
This leads to the formation of subareolar abscess, dilation, and eventually, the rupture of the duct, causing fistulas.

**Duct Ectasia:** This is a benign (non-cancerous) condition where the milk ducts in the breast widen and thicken. This can cause a blockage and a build-up of fluid, which often appears as a sticky, green, black, or grey discharge from the nipple.

blocks.text: The most likely diagnosis in this patient with recent trauma and calcification could be fat necrosis. Breast fat necrosis is caused by injured or ischemic breast tissue that is replaced with scar tissue and presents as a palpable nodule. It is commonly caused by breast trauma and breast surgical procedures. It presents as a mammographic density, a painless palpable lump, skin thickening, or deposits of calcium.

Fat necrosis can manifest in a variety of ways that closely resemble cancer like irregular breast mass, usually fixed to the dermis, with possible skin tethering and/or nipple retraction as a result of fibrotic bands between necrotic tissue and skin. Calcifications can sometimes occur in fat necrosis, particularly in older lesions.
These are typically punctate (tiny dots) and scattered throughout the lump, unlike some cancers (differentiated by biopsy).

items.text: **Mastitis(Option A):** This is an infection of breast tissue, often caused by bacteria entering through milk ducts during breastfeeding. It can cause inflammation, redness, pain, fever, and chills, which are absent in this case.

**Breast Abscess(Option B):** This is a localized collection of pus within the breast tissue, often caused by a bacterial infection. It presents with fever, chills, and a more fluctuant (fluid-filled) mass compared to the firm mass often felt with fat necrosis.
**Inflammatory Breast Cancer(Option D):** It typically presents with additional symptoms like skin thickening, peau d'orange (skin resembling an orange peel), and rapid progression.

blocks.text: The clinical features and HPE showing central sclerosis with fibroelastotic stroma and entrapped glands radiating outwards with hyperplasia are suggestive of radial scar. Radial scars, also known as complex sclerosing lesions, are benign proliferative breast lesions that can mimic breast cancer clinically and radiologically but look like scars when viewed under a microscope.
They are characterized by a spiculated appearance on imaging, with a translucent, low-density center.
Grossly, a whitish scar is present at the center (central stellate scar).
HPE shows glands entrapped in a hyalinised stroma surrounded by long radiating projections containing epithelium.

The above features of cyclical pain and breast changes are suggestive of fibrocystic breast disease, which has a blue dome of Bloodgood cyst. Fibrocystic changes of the breast is a benign condition characterized by the development of cysts, fibrosis (thickening and scarring of tissue), and other benign alterations in the breast tissue.
**Symptoms:**

items.text: Breast pain (mastalgia) or tenderness that fluctuates with menstruation

Mastalgia (or mastodynia) can be cyclic (with menses, due to premenstrual edema) or noncyclic (localized to one area of the breast and may be caused by ruptured cysts, physical injury, and infections).
Breast lumps or nodules
Swelling or enlargement of the breasts
Fluid-filled cysts with varying size
Nipple discharge

blocks.text: **Gross Features:** Blue-domed cyst of Bloodgood- Large cysts that contain turbid, semitranslucent brown or blue-colored fluid which imparts a blue color onto the intact cyst. They are typically fluid-filled and may vary in size.
**Histopathological Features:**

items.text: **Cysts:** Fluid-filled sacs within the breast tissue, often surrounded by fibrous tissue.
**Fibrosis:** Thickening and scarring of breast tissue, which may result in palpable lumps or areas of increased density on imaging studies.
**Apocrine Metaplasia:** Transformation of ductal epithelial cells into apocrine-like cells, characterized by abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and apical snouts.

blocks.text: The histopathology image shows epithelial ducts compressed and distorted by surrounding stroma which is characteristic of an intracanalicular fibroadenoma.
The FNAC features of a fibroadenoma include:

items.text: Staghorn clusters of cells - Ductal cells arranged in a deer horn-like pattern.
Bare nuclei - cytoplasm is stripped off and only nuclei are visible in blue color.

blocks.text: **Intracanalicular Fibroadenoma:**
**Other features of Fibroadenoma:**

items.text: Fibroadenoma is the most common benign breast tumor, typically found in women aged 15-35.
Spherical masses measuring 1-10 cm, firm, non-tender, well-circumscribed, mobile, and often single.
The lump is mobile and slippery and hence called breast mouse.
**Estrogen sensitivity:** Can increase in size during pregnancy, lactation, or estrogen therapy, and usually regress after menopause.

blocks.text: **Histopathology:**

items.text: Well-defined borders due to a fibrous capsule, with proliferating stroma potentially compressing and distorting glandular components.
Popcorn calcification on mammograms.
**Aging effect:** Epithelium atrophies with age, and the stroma becomes more hyalinized.

blocks.text: **Molecular alteration:** Alterations in MED12 gene
**Drug associated with bilateral fibroadenomas:** Cyclosporine ( A calcineurin inhibitor)
**Management:** Surgical excision
**Indications for surgical excision:**

items.text: Age >30 years
Size >5 cm
Microlobulation on imaging
Atypia on histology
Family history of breast cancer, and
The patient’s preference

blocks.text: Complex fibroadenoma is an example of epithelial proliferative breast lesions without atypia. Fibroadenoma with complex features has a risk of malignancy, whereas, without complexity, it does not.
Complex features include:

items.text: Cysts > 0.3cm
Sclerosing adenosis (sclerosis + increase in the acini cells per lobule i.e, adenosis)
Epithelial calcifications
Papillary apocrine change (metaplastic change in breast tissue)
